result.title: The score that lied
result.outcome: With one curated docs file, the small model's task success went from 11% to 89% and the large model's from 84% to 100%. Fetching the live docs did not come close.
numbers: 11% to 89% task success on the small model, once it had the docs file
360 runs: 15 tasks, 4 conditions, 2 models, 3 runs each
result.text:
The wrong first answer

The question was simple: are our docs ready for AI agents? My first answer was a score. It rated how agent-ready a doc page looked.

My manager asked why I trusted it. I did not have a good answer. The score measured whether a page looked right to me, not whether an agent could use it to get work done. I had built it, which made me the last person likely to question it. I scrapped it.

What I built instead

An eval that asks coding agents to do real Pinecone work and checks whether the code they write actually runs. Pass or fail, no partial credit.

There are 15 developer tasks, such as creating an index or migrating a legacy one. Each task runs under four conditions:

1. No docs. The agent works from what it already knows.
2. A curated docs file. One short page that shows the right way to do common tasks.
3. The live docs, through MCP.
4. The live docs, through web fetch, the way a browser would load them.

Every task ran three times per condition on two models, Claude Haiku 4.5 (the small model) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (the large model). That is 360 runs.

What happened

| Condition | Small model | Large model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No docs | 11% | 84% |
| Curated docs file | 89% | 100% |
| Live docs through MCP | 4% | 51% |
| Live docs through web fetch | 18% | 84% |

The docs file was the only condition that clearly helped. The small model went from 5 passing runs out of 45 to 40 out of 45. The large model went from 84% to every run passing.

The live docs did not help. Through MCP, both models did worse than with no docs at all. Through web fetch, the large model scored exactly what it scored with nothing, and the small model gained seven points.

None of this says the live docs were badly written. They were written for people browsing a site, and they do that job. The docs file carries the same knowledge in a shape an agent can apply directly.

What it taught me

The shape of what an agent reads mattered more than the channel it arrived through. The two channels did differ from each other, but the better one got the small model to 18%. The same knowledge in a different shape got it to 89%. My recommendation was to bring the patterns from the docs file into the regular docs, so an agent lands on them whatever route it takes.

The cheaper model gained the most. The large model already knew most of the answers. The small model knew almost none of them, and one page took it to nearly all. If more agent work runs on cheaper models, that gap is where the writing pays off.

The first lesson came before any of this, and it was mine. I built a metric, liked it, and needed my manager to ask the obvious question before I checked it against real work.

I later presented this work in my Salesforce interviews.

content.text:
At Pinecone in 2026, Andrew built an eval that gave coding agents 15 real developer tasks and checked whether the code they wrote actually ran. Each run was a plain pass or fail. **One short curated docs file helped far more than anything else. Pointing the agents at the live docs did not help.**

**Models:** Claude Haiku 4.5 (small) and Claude Sonnet 4.6 (large). There were 360 runs in total: 15 tasks × 4 conditions × 2 models × 3 runs each.

| Condition | Haiku 4.5 | Sonnet 4.6 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No docs | 11% | 84% |
| Curated docs file | 89% | 100% |
| Live docs through MCP | 4% | 51% |
| Live docs through web fetch | 18% | 84% |

- **Haiku:** with the docs file it went from 5 of 45 runs passing to 40 of 45.
- **Sonnet:** with the docs file every run passed.
- **MCP:** both models did worse than with no docs at all.
- **Web fetch:** Sonnet scored the same as with no docs, and Haiku gained 7 points.

**What he concluded:** The way the information was laid out mattered more than how the agent got to it. He recommended adding the docs file's patterns to the regular docs. The smaller, cheaper model gained the most.

Source: [The score that lied](https://andrewyu.app/work/the-score-that-lied)
